title: Amazon EKS in Production
subtitle: IAM, Terraform, security, Karpenter, storage, observability and upgrades
description: Run Amazon EKS the way production demands: per-workload IAM with IRSA and Pod Identity, clusters as Terraform, locked-down networking and secrets, Karpenter and Spot economics, EBS/EFS storage, CloudWatch and Prometheus observability, and a repeatable upgrade, backup and troubleshooting runbook.
outcomes: Give every pod least-privilege AWS access and prove it
Provision and upgrade an EKS cluster with Terraform
Secure, scale and observe the cluster and recover from failures

modules.title: Identity and provisioning
modules.summary: Give workloads their own AWS identity and build the cluster as code.

lessons.title: Workload IAM: IRSA and EKS Pod Identity
lessons.summary: Give pods their own least-privilege AWS identity, using IRSA or EKS Pod Identity, and prove it from inside a pod.
objectives: Explain why pods must not inherit the node instance role
Compare IRSA and EKS Pod Identity and choose between them
Write an IAM trust policy, a ServiceAccount annotation and a Pod Identity association
Verify the identity a pod really uses with aws sts get-caller-identity

sections.title: What you will build and the path through this course
sections.body:
This course takes you from a working EKS cluster (the prerequisite course *Amazon EKS essentials*) to one you can run in production. The path is: **identity** (this lesson) -> **provisioning as code** with Terraform -> **networking and security** -> **scaling and cost** -> **storage** -> **observability** -> **upgrades, backup and troubleshooting**. Each lesson builds on the previous one: the Terraform module you write in lesson 2 creates the OIDC provider and add-ons used by every later lesson.

We start with identity because every other production feature (autoscaling, storage drivers, external secrets, log shipping) is a pod that calls AWS APIs, and each needs credentials. Getting this right first prevents the most common EKS security mistake: giving every pod the permissions of the worker node.

A worker node is an EC2 instance with an **instance profile** (an IAM role attached to the VM). Any process on the node, including every pod, can reach the **instance metadata service (IMDS)** at 169.254.169.254 and obtain the temporary credentials of that role. If the node role can read S3 or Secrets Manager, so can every pod, including a compromised one.

The fix is to give each workload its own IAM role through its Kubernetes **ServiceAccount** (the identity a pod runs as inside the cluster), and to keep the node role minimal (only what the kubelet and CNI need). EKS offers two mechanisms: **IRSA** (IAM Roles for Service Accounts, uses an OIDC identity provider) and **EKS Pod Identity** (newer, uses an agent on each node and an EKS API association).

sections.title: IRSA versus EKS Pod Identity
head: Aspect
IRSA
EKS Pod Identity
rows: Projected OIDC token in the pod; AWS STS AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
Federated: the cluster's OIDC provider ARN, with a sub condition per namespace:serviceaccount
Service principal pods.eks.amazonaws.com (same for all clusters)
No annotation; an EKS association links namespace + ServiceAccount to a role
Trust policy must name each cluster's OIDC issuer, so roles are not reusable across clusters
Role is reusable across clusters; no trust policy edit per cluster
EC2, Fargate, EKS Anywhere, self-managed clusters
EC2 nodes only (not Fargate, not EKS Anywhere)
Cluster name, namespace and ServiceAccount are added as tags for ABAC
One OIDC provider per cluster; 100 OIDC providers per account by default

sections.title: About this example: the IRSA IAM trust policy
sections.body: This is the **trust policy** of an IAM role named `orders-s3-reader`, the document that says who may assume the role. It is not a Kubernetes file, so it is shown as plain text; you attach it with `aws iam create-role --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json`. Look at the `Federated` principal (your cluster's OIDC provider ARN) and the `sub` condition, which restricts the role to exactly one ServiceAccount in one namespace: without that condition, any ServiceAccount in the cluster could assume the role.

sections.title: IRSA trust policy (trust.json)
sections.note: Always pin both aud and sub with StringEquals. A StringLike with a wildcard sub is a common over-permissive shortcut.

sections.title: About this example: ServiceAccount and test pod for IRSA
sections.body: This manifest creates the `orders-api` ServiceAccount with the annotation naming the role ARN, and a pod that runs the AWS CLI image under it. You apply it with `kubectl apply -f`. The annotation is what makes the EKS pod identity webhook inject the `AWS_ROLE_ARN` and `AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE` variables and a projected token volume into the pod; check the `serviceAccountName` field in the pod, since a pod that does not name it silently falls back to the default ServiceAccount and gets no role.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: orders
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/orders-s3-reader
    eks.amazonaws.com/sts-regional-endpoints: "true"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: aws-cli-test
  namespace: orders
spec:
  serviceAccountName: orders-api
  restartPolicy: Never
  containers:
    - name: aws
      image: amazon/aws-cli:2.17.0
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
sections.title: ServiceAccount annotated for IRSA, plus a verification pod
sections.note: The webhook only mutates pods created after the annotation exists. Restart existing pods after adding it.

sections.title: About this example: EKS Pod Identity setup and verification
sections.body: These are the AWS CLI and kubectl commands to use Pod Identity instead. The first installs the `eks-pod-identity-agent` add-on, the second creates the **association** (it links the `orders` namespace and `orders-api` ServiceAccount to a role, with no annotation needed), and the last two prove the result from inside the pod. In the output, the `Arn` of `get-caller-identity` must show `assumed-role/orders-s3-reader` with a session name, never the node role (`eks-node-role`).

sections.code:
kubectl -n orders exec aws-cli-test -- env | grep -E 'AWS_(ROLE|WEB|CONTAINER|REGION)'
kubectl -n orders get pod aws-cli-test -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}{"\n"}'
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text
sections.title: Which credential source is the pod using?
sections.note: The last line runs on your laptop, not in the pod: it is the identity of the human, shown for contrast.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** Leaving IMDS reachable: set the node group metadata option `http_put_response_hop_limit = 1` so pods cannot reach node credentials. **2.** Forgetting `serviceAccountName`, so the pod runs as `default`. **3.** A trust policy `sub` that does not match `system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>` exactly (typos give `AccessDenied` from `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`). **4.** Using an old SDK that does not support the container credentials provider or web identity. **5.** Attaching `AdministratorAccess` to the workload role to make an error disappear.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Pods inherit the node role unless you give them an identity. **IRSA** uses the cluster OIDC provider, a trust policy with an `aud`/`sub` condition and an annotated ServiceAccount; **Pod Identity** uses an agent add-on and an association, and produces roles that are reusable across clusters. Prefer Pod Identity on EC2 nodes, keep IRSA for Fargate and other clusters, and always verify with `aws sts get-caller-identity` from inside the pod.

Next you will codify the cluster itself, including the OIDC provider, the Pod Identity add-on and these IAM roles, with Terraform.

exercises.title: Prove the identity
exercises.prompt: Run `aws sts get-caller-identity` from inside a pod and confirm it is an assumed role for the workload, not the node role.
exercises.command: kubectl -n orders exec aws-cli-test -- aws sts get-caller-identity
exercises.hint: If the Arn shows the node role, check serviceAccountName and the association or annotation.
exercises.solution: Confirm with: kubectl -n orders get pod aws-cli-test -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}', then recreate the pod after fixing the annotation or association.

exercises.title: List associations
exercises.prompt: List all Pod Identity associations of the cluster and find the one for orders-api.
exercises.expected: An association entry for namespace orders and serviceAccount orders-api.

questions.question: Why is relying on the node instance role dangerous?
options: Every pod on the node can obtain the role's credentials through IMDS
questions.explain: All pods on a node can reach IMDS, so one compromised pod gets all node permissions.

questions.question: Which statement about EKS Pod Identity is true?
options: It needs an OIDC provider per cluster
The role trust principal is pods.eks.amazonaws.com
questions.explain: Pod Identity uses the service principal pods.eks.amazonaws.com and an EKS association, no annotation.

questions.question: What does the sub condition in an IRSA trust policy do?
options: Restricts the role to one namespace and ServiceAccount
questions.explain: sub is system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>, which limits who can assume the role.

questions.question: A pod returns the node role from get-caller-identity. First check?
options: That the pod uses the intended serviceAccountName and was created after the annotation or association
questions.explain: A pod on the default ServiceAccount, or created before the mutation, will not receive the workload role.

lessons.title: Provisioning EKS with Terraform
lessons.summary: Codify a production EKS cluster with the community module: VPC, managed node groups, add-ons, access entries and outputs.
objectives: Structure a Terraform project for EKS with remote state
Configure terraform-aws-modules/eks with managed node groups and core add-ons
Grant cluster access with access entries instead of aws-auth
Plan, apply and connect kubectl using module outputs

sections.title: Why Terraform, and how the project is laid out
sections.body:
Clicking through the console or running `eksctl` is fine to learn, but a production cluster must be **reproducible, reviewable and diffable**. **Terraform** (version 1.6 or newer here) describes infrastructure in HCL files, compares them to a **state file** and applies only the difference. The **AWS provider 5.x** talks to AWS, and the community module `terraform-aws-modules/eks/aws` (v20) wraps the dozens of resources an EKS cluster needs: control plane, IAM roles, security groups, OIDC provider, node groups, add-ons and access entries.

A typical layout has one directory per environment (`envs/prod`) with `versions.tf` (pinned providers and a remote backend), `vpc.tf`, `eks.tf` and `outputs.tf`. State lives in an S3 bucket with DynamoDB locking so two engineers cannot apply at once.

sections.title: Main module inputs
head: Argument
Meaning
Example
rows: Name and Kubernetes minor version of the control plane
VPC and private subnets for nodes and control plane ENIs
Whether the API endpoint is reachable from the internet
Map of EKS add-ons (CoreDNS, kube-proxy, VPC CNI, Pod Identity agent, EBS CSI)
Map of managed node groups (AWS manages AMI rollout and draining)
Map of IAM principals granted Kubernetes access
Give the identity running Terraform admin access
Control plane log streams sent to CloudWatch

sections.title: About this example: versions.tf and the VPC
sections.body: This file pins Terraform and the AWS provider, stores state remotely, and creates a three-AZ VPC with the community VPC module. The subnet tags matter: `kubernetes.io/role/internal-elb` lets the AWS Load Balancer Controller place internal load balancers, and `karpenter.sh/discovery` (used in lesson 4) lets Karpenter find subnets. Read `private_subnets`: nodes live there and reach the internet through NAT gateways.

sections.title: versions.tf and vpc.tf
sections.note: Large private subnets (/19) matter: with the VPC CNI every pod consumes a VPC IP, so small subnets cause IP exhaustion (lesson 7).

sections.title: About this example: the EKS module call
sections.body: This is `eks.tf`, the heart of the project. It creates a 1.31 control plane with a private-plus-restricted public endpoint, core add-ons, one managed node group for system workloads, and **access entries**, the current replacement for editing the `aws-auth` ConfigMap. Notice `before_compute = true` on the VPC CNI (it must exist before nodes join), the `AmazonEKSClusterAdminPolicy` association for the platform team, and `enable_irsa = true` which creates the OIDC provider from lesson 1.

sections.title: eks.tf
sections.note: authentication_mode = "API" uses access entries only. Use "API_AND_CONFIG_MAP" while migrating an older cluster that still relies on aws-auth.

sections.title: About this example: init, plan, apply and connecting
sections.body: This is the command sequence you run from `envs/prod`, after adding an `outputs.tf` that exposes `module.eks.cluster_name`, `cluster_endpoint` and `oidc_provider_arn` (other stacks read them, for example the IAM roles from lesson 1). `init` downloads providers and modules, `plan` shows a diff you must read, `apply` creates resources (about 12 to 15 minutes) and `aws eks update-kubeconfig` writes your kubectl context. Look at the plan totals: `Plan: 61 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy` is expected on a first run, while any `to destroy` on an existing cluster deserves scrutiny; then check that `kubectl get nodes` shows Ready nodes.

sections.code:
terraform init
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
aws eks update-kubeconfig --region us-east-1 --name prod-eks
kubectl get nodes

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** Local state: two people apply at once and corrupt the cluster record; use the S3 backend with locking. **2.** Unpinned module versions: `terraform init -upgrade` can silently change a production cluster. **3.** Bumping `cluster_version` by two minors in one commit; EKS only upgrades one minor at a time. **4.** Losing admin access because `enable_cluster_creator_admin_permissions = false` and no access entry matches you. **5.** Public endpoint open to `0.0.0.0/0`. **6.** Putting application manifests in the same state as the cluster.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
You pinned Terraform and the provider, created a three-AZ VPC, called the EKS module with managed node groups, core add-ons and **access entries**, and used outputs plus `update-kubeconfig` to connect. Everything is in version control and repeatable.

Next we secure the network layer of this cluster: security groups for pods, network policies, private endpoints, secrets and KMS encryption.

exercises.hint: The summary is the last line of the plan output.

exercises.title: Connect to the cluster
exercises.prompt: Create the kubeconfig entry from the module output and list nodes.
exercises.expected: Added new context ... and kubectl get nodes lists Ready nodes.
exercises.hint: Use terraform output configure_kubectl to get the exact command.
exercises.solution: eval "$(terraform output -raw configure_kubectl)" && kubectl get nodes

questions.question: What replaces editing the aws-auth ConfigMap in modern EKS?
questions.explain: Access entries are managed through the EKS API and can be defined in Terraform.

questions.question: Why store Terraform state in S3 with DynamoDB?
options: Shared state and locking prevent concurrent corruption
questions.explain: Remote state with locking lets a team apply safely.

questions.question: Why is before_compute = true set on the vpc-cni add-on?
options: Nodes need the CNI before they can join and become Ready
It sets the endpoint to private
questions.explain: Without a CNI, nodes cannot start pods and stay NotReady.

questions.question: How many Kubernetes minor versions can one EKS upgrade jump?
questions.explain: EKS control plane upgrades are one minor version at a time.

modules.title: Security, scaling and storage
modules.summary: Harden the network, scale economically and run stateful data.

lessons.title: Networking and security on EKS
lessons.summary: Isolate pods with security groups and network policies, lock down the API endpoint, and manage secrets and encryption with AWS services.
objectives: Explain how the VPC CNI gives pods VPC IPs and what that means for security groups
Apply a SecurityGroupPolicy and a NetworkPolicy enforced by the VPC CNI
Choose between public, restricted and private cluster endpoints
Sync secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and encrypt Kubernetes secrets with KMS

sections.title: Layers of isolation in an EKS cluster
sections.body: EKS gives you four independent layers, and production clusters use all of them. **Pod networking**: the **Amazon VPC CNI** plugin gives each pod a real VPC IP address from the node's ENIs, so pods are first-class citizens of the VPC. **Network policy**: Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` objects, enforced by the VPC CNI when you enable its network policy agent (an eBPF-based enforcer, Kubernetes 1.25+ and VPC CNI 1.14+). **Security groups for pods**: AWS security groups attached to individual pods, useful when the target is an RDS database that only accepts traffic from a specific security group. **Endpoint and data protection**: who can reach the API server, where secrets come from, and how they are encrypted at rest.

sections.title: Which control for which problem
head: Need
Use
Where configured
rows: Allow only the orders pods to reach RDS
Deny all traffic into a namespace by default
Enable enableNetworkPolicy: "true" in the vpc-cni add-on configuration
Restrict who can call the API server
Endpoint access settings and CIDR allow-list
Keep database passwords out of Git
Secrets Manager + External Secrets Operator or CSI driver
Encrypt Secret objects in etcd with your own key
encryptionConfig on the cluster (cluster_encryption_config in Terraform)

sections.title: About this example: SecurityGroupPolicy and NetworkPolicy
sections.body: This file holds two complete manifests. The `SecurityGroupPolicy` attaches security group `sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890` (allowed by the RDS security group) to pods labelled `app: orders`; it needs the VPC CNI setting `ENABLE_POD_ENI=true` and a supported Nitro instance type. The `NetworkPolicy` is a default-deny ingress policy for the `orders` namespace plus an allow rule from `ingress-nginx`; apply with `kubectl apply -f`, and notice the empty `podSelector: {}` which selects every pod.

sections.code:
apiVersion: vpcresources.k8s.aws/v1beta1
kind: SecurityGroupPolicy
metadata:
  name: orders-db-access
  namespace: orders
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  securityGroups:
    groupIds:
      - sg-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: orders
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-from-ingress
  namespace: orders
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
sections.title: SecurityGroupPolicy plus NetworkPolicies
sections.note: To turn the enforcer on, update the add-on: aws eks update-addon --cluster-name prod-eks --addon-name vpc-cni --configuration-values '{"enableNetworkPolicy":"true"}'. Without it NetworkPolicy objects are accepted but silently not enforced.

sections.title: About this example: ExternalSecret from Secrets Manager
sections.body: The External Secrets Operator (installed by Helm, using Pod Identity for AWS access) reads a secret from **AWS Secrets Manager** and writes a normal Kubernetes Secret. The `ClusterSecretStore` says how to authenticate and where, and the `ExternalSecret` says which remote key becomes which Secret and how often to refresh it. Apply both with `kubectl apply -f`, then read the `STATUS` column of `kubectl get externalsecret`, which must say `SecretSynced`. The alternative, the Secrets Store CSI Driver with the AWS provider, mounts the value as a file and avoids creating a Secret object at all.

sections.code:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets-manager
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: orders-db
  namespace: orders
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: aws-secrets-manager
  target:
    name: orders-db
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/orders/db
        property: password
sections.title: ClusterSecretStore and ExternalSecret
sections.output:
clustersecretstore.external-secrets.io/aws-secrets-manager created
externalsecret.external-secrets.io/orders-db created

$ kubectl -n orders get externalsecret
NAME        STORE                 REFRESH INTERVAL   STATUS         READY
orders-db   aws-secrets-manager   1h                 SecretSynced   True
sections.note: The operator's own role needs secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and DescribeSecret only on arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-1:123456789012:secret:prod/orders/*.

sections.title: About this example: checking endpoint and encryption settings
sections.body: This command reads the cluster description and extracts the three settings that define its exposure: endpoint access, allowed CIDRs and KMS encryption. The matching Terraform arguments are `cluster_endpoint_public_access`, `cluster_endpoint_public_access_cidrs` and `cluster_encryption_config = { resources = ["secrets"], provider_key_arn = aws_kms_key.eks.arn }`. In the output, look at `endpointPublicAccess`: `false` means a private cluster, reachable only from inside the VPC, peered networks, a VPN or Direct Connect, and in that case you also need VPC interface endpoints (ecr.api, ecr.dkr, sts, s3 gateway) so private nodes can pull images and call AWS.

sections.code:
aws eks describe-cluster --name prod-eks \
  --query 'cluster.{endpoint:resourcesVpcConfig,encryption:encryptionConfig}' --output json
sections.title: Inspect endpoint access and encryption
sections.note: Envelope encryption can be enabled on an existing cluster but never removed, so pick the CMK carefully and enable key rotation.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** Writing NetworkPolicies without enabling the VPC CNI network policy agent: they look applied but nothing is enforced. **2.** A default-deny policy without an egress rule for DNS (UDP/TCP 53 to kube-system) breaks name resolution. **3.** Security groups for pods on unsupported instance types or without `ENABLE_POD_ENI`. **4.** Private endpoint with no route from your CI runner, locking the pipeline out. **5.** Storing the secret value in Git instead of only its Secrets Manager key name. **6.** Believing KMS encryption hides secrets from users with `get secret` RBAC; it protects data at rest only.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Pods have VPC IPs, which lets you use security groups per pod and NetworkPolicies enforced by the VPC CNI. Restrict or privatise the API endpoint, source secrets from Secrets Manager through External Secrets or the CSI driver, and encrypt Secret objects with a KMS key.

With a secure baseline in place, the next lesson makes the cluster elastic: autoscaling with Karpenter, spot capacity and cost control.

questions.question: What must be enabled for NetworkPolicy objects to take effect with the VPC CNI?
options: The network policy agent via enableNetworkPolicy
questions.explain: The VPC CNI add-on must have enableNetworkPolicy set to true.

questions.question: Security groups for pods require which pod-level resource?
questions.explain: A SecurityGroupPolicy selects pods and attaches SG ids.

questions.question: A private-only API endpoint means...

questions.explain: endpointPublicAccess false restricts access to private networks.

questions.question: What does KMS envelope encryption on EKS protect?
questions.explain: With encryptionConfig, Secret objects in etcd are encrypted with your CMK.

lessons.title: Scaling and cost: Karpenter, Spot and right-sizing
lessons.summary: Scale nodes automatically with Karpenter or Cluster Autoscaler, use Spot safely, and make EKS costs visible.
objectives: Compare Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter and pick one
Write a Karpenter NodePool and EC2NodeClass for on-demand and Spot capacity
Make workloads Spot-tolerant and right-size their requests
Attribute cost to namespaces and teams

sections.title: Two layers of scaling, and who owns the nodes
sections.body:
Scaling on Kubernetes happens at two layers. **Pod scaling** (HorizontalPodAutoscaler, covered in the Operations course) changes the number of replicas. **Node scaling** changes the number of EC2 instances so that all pods have somewhere to run. Node scaling reacts to **Pending pods** that no node can fit.

On EKS there are two mainstream node autoscalers. **Cluster Autoscaler** (CA) scales pre-defined Auto Scaling Groups (managed node groups) up and down. **Karpenter** has no node groups: it reads the pending pods' requests, picks the cheapest EC2 instance types that fit (including Spot) from a wide list, launches them directly and consolidates (replaces or removes) nodes that are underused. Karpenter itself runs on a small managed node group, never on nodes it manages.

sections.title: Cluster Autoscaler versus Karpenter
head: Aspect
Cluster Autoscaler
Karpenter
rows: Node group (ASG) with a fixed instance type list
Individual instances chosen per pending pod batch
Typically under a minute to a node
You pre-create a group per shape
Dynamic, from NodePool requirements (families, sizes, Spot or on-demand)
Removes nodes below a utilisation threshold
Consolidation: delete empty or underused nodes and repack
NodePool and EC2NodeClass custom resources (API karpenter.sh/v1)
One Spot group per diversification set
Mixes Spot and on-demand, handles interruption messages through SQS
Simple, static shapes, strict ASG governance

sections.title: About this example: NodePool and EC2NodeClass
sections.body: These two manifests are Karpenter v1 resources. The **EC2NodeClass** describes the AWS side: which IAM role the nodes use, which subnets and security groups (found by the `karpenter.sh/discovery` tag you set in Terraform), and which AMI (`al2023@latest`). The **NodePool** describes the Kubernetes side: allowed capacity types, instance categories, a CPU limit as a spending guard, and the consolidation policy. Check `limits.cpu`, which caps total provisioned vCPU, and `expireAfter`, which forces periodic node replacement so AMI patches roll out.

sections.code:
apiVersion: karpenter.k8s.aws/v1
kind: EC2NodeClass
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  role: KarpenterNodeRole-prod-eks
  amiSelectorTerms:
    - alias: al2023@latest
  subnetSelectorTerms:
    - tags:
        karpenter.sh/discovery: prod-eks
  securityGroupSelectorTerms:
    - tags:
        karpenter.sh/discovery: prod-eks
  metadataOptions:
    httpTokens: required
    httpPutResponseHopLimit: 1
  blockDeviceMappings:
    - deviceName: /dev/xvda
      ebs:
        volumeSize: 50Gi
        volumeType: gp3
        encrypted: true
---
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1
kind: NodePool
metadata:
  name: general
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeClassRef:
        group: karpenter.k8s.aws
        kind: EC2NodeClass
        name: default
      requirements:
        - key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type
          operator: In
          values: ["spot", "on-demand"]
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category
          operator: In
          values: ["c", "m", "r"]
        - key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-generation
          operator: Gt
          values: ["4"]
        - key: kubernetes.io/arch
          operator: In
          values: ["amd64"]
      expireAfter: 720h
  limits:
    cpu: "200"
  disruption:
    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
    consolidateAfter: 1m
sections.title: Karpenter EC2NodeClass and NodePool
sections.note: Karpenter prefers Spot when both are allowed because it is cheaper. Create a separate on-demand NodePool for critical workloads and select it with a nodeSelector.

sections.title: About this example: watching Karpenter scale
sections.body: This session creates a Deployment of pause containers with a CPU request, scales it up beyond the current capacity, and then watches Karpenter react. The pause pods do nothing but reserve resources, which makes this a safe load test. Look at the Karpenter log lines `found provisionable pod(s)` and `launched nodeclaim`, which show the chosen instance types and capacity type, and at the new nodes appearing in `kubectl get nodes` with their `karpenter.sh/capacity-type` label.

sections.code:
kubectl create deployment inflate --image=public.ecr.aws/eks-distro/kubernetes/pause:3.7 --replicas=0
kubectl set resources deployment inflate --requests=cpu=1
kubectl scale deployment inflate --replicas=20
kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/karpenter -f --tail=5
kubectl get nodes -L karpenter.sh/capacity-type,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type
sections.title: Trigger and observe a scale-up
sections.note: Scale the deployment back to 0 afterwards; within about a minute consolidation removes the empty Spot nodes.

sections.title: About this example: a Spot-tolerant workload
sections.body: This is a complete Deployment designed for Spot and for consolidation. Spot instances can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning, so it runs three replicas, spreads them across zones with a `topologySpreadConstraints` rule, protects availability with a PodDisruptionBudget, and sets `requests` equal to what the app really needs. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f`; the `requests` block is the one that drives both scheduling and Karpenter's choice of instance size, so over-asking here directly increases your bill.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: orders
    team: payments
    cost-center: cc-1042
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders
        team: payments
        cost-center: cc-1042
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: orders
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/orders-api:1.8.2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 384Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: orders
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
sections.title: Spot-friendly Deployment and PodDisruptionBudget
sections.output:
deployment.apps/orders-api created
poddisruptionbudget.policy/orders-api created

$ kubectl -n orders top pods
NAME                          CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
orders-api-7f9c5d8b64-2kq9x   41m          212Mi
orders-api-7f9c5d8b64-8wzr5   38m          205Mi
orders-api-7f9c5d8b64-m4c7t   44m          219Mi
sections.note: Here actual CPU use is about 40m against a 250m request: this is the signal that the workload is over-provisioned (see right-sizing in the table above and the callout below).

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** Running Karpenter on nodes that Karpenter itself manages: if they are consolidated, nothing can scale. **2.** Running single-replica or stateful workloads on Spot without a PDB or graceful shutdown. **3.** Omitting `limits.cpu` in the NodePool, so a runaway Deployment buys hundreds of instances. **4.** Setting `requests` far above real usage; use `kubectl top`, Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode, or Goldilocks. **5.** No cost labels, so the bill cannot be split by team. **6.** Pinning one instance type; wider choice means more Spot availability. For cost visibility, activate `team` and `cost-center` as cost allocation tags in Billing and install OpenCost or Kubecost for per-namespace numbers.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Karpenter provisions right-sized nodes directly from pending pods and consolidates them, using Spot where safe; Cluster Autoscaler is the simpler ASG-based alternative. Spot works when workloads have several replicas, a PDB, zone spread and short shutdown times. Right-size requests from measured usage and tag everything for cost allocation.

Next: stateful data, with EBS and EFS CSI drivers, StorageClasses and snapshots.

exercises.title: Check capacity types

exercises.expected: A table with spot or on-demand per node.
exercises.hint: Nodes in the managed system group show an empty capacity-type label.
exercises.solution: Use -L with comma separated label keys.

exercises.title: Find over-provisioning
exercises.prompt: Compare actual usage with requests for the orders namespace.
exercises.expected: CPU and memory columns well below the requested values signal waste.
exercises.hint: Compare against kubectl -n orders get pods -o custom-columns for requests.
exercises.solution: Lower requests toward p95 usage plus headroom, then watch for throttling or OOMKilled.

questions.question: What triggers Karpenter to launch a node?
questions.explain: Karpenter provisions capacity for pods that cannot be scheduled.

questions.question: What does NodePool limits.cpu do?
options: Caps the total vCPU Karpenter may provision
questions.explain: It is a spending guard on total capacity.

questions.question: Which setup makes a Deployment safe on Spot?
options: Several replicas, PDB, zone spread, graceful shutdown
questions.explain: Spot reclaim gives two minutes of notice, so the app must tolerate losing a node.

questions.question: Where does Karpenter itself run?

lessons.title: Storage and data: EBS, EFS and snapshots
lessons.summary: Choose between EBS and EFS, define StorageClasses, and protect volumes with CSI snapshots.
objectives: Explain the zonal nature of EBS and the shared nature of EFS
Write StorageClasses for gp3 EBS and EFS access points
Create a VolumeSnapshot and restore it into a new PVC
Avoid the stuck-in-wrong-zone Pending pod problem

sections.title: Two storage services, two very different behaviours
sections.body:
Kubernetes asks for storage with a **PersistentVolumeClaim** (PVC), and a **StorageClass** says how to provision it. On EKS the provisioning is done by **CSI drivers** (Container Storage Interface plugins) that you install as EKS add-ons: `aws-ebs-csi-driver` and `aws-efs-csi-driver`. The drivers need AWS permissions, so give them an IAM role through Pod Identity or IRSA as in lesson 1.

**EBS** is block storage: fast, one pod at a time (`ReadWriteOnce`), and **bound to a single Availability Zone**. **EFS** is a managed NFS file system: shared by many pods and nodes across zones (`ReadWriteMany`), slower per operation, billed per GB used.

sections.title: EBS versus EFS
head: Aspect
EBS (gp3)
EFS
rows: Provisioned IOPS and throughput (gp3 baseline 3000 IOPS)
Elastic or provisioned throughput, higher latency
Shared uploads, CMS content, ML datasets
Dynamic via access points, or static to an existing file system
Use AWS Backup; no CSI snapshots

sections.title: About this example: StorageClasses and a PVC
sections.body: This file defines a default gp3 StorageClass for EBS, an EFS StorageClass that creates one **access point** per volume, and a PVC. `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer` is the important field for EBS: the volume is only created after the pod is scheduled, in the same zone as the node, which prevents a volume being created in a zone where the pod cannot run. For EFS replace `fs-0123456789abcdef0` with your file system ID; apply with `kubectl apply -f`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: gp3
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
  kmsKeyId: arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
  iops: "4000"
  throughput: "250"
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true
reclaimPolicy: Delete
---
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: efs-shared
provisioner: efs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  provisioningMode: efs-ap
  fileSystemId: fs-0123456789abcdef0
  directoryPerms: "700"
reclaimPolicy: Retain
volumeBindingMode: Immediate
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pg-data
  namespace: orders
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
sections.title: StorageClasses for EBS gp3 and EFS, and a PVC
sections.output:
storageclass.storage.k8s.io/gp3 created
storageclass.storage.k8s.io/efs-shared created
persistentvolumeclaim/pg-data created

$ kubectl get sc
NAME            PROVISIONER       RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE
gp3 (default)   ebs.csi.aws.com   Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer   true                   4s
efs-shared      efs.csi.aws.com   Retain          Immediate              false                  4s
gp2             kubernetes.io/aws-ebs   Delete    WaitForFirstConsumer   false                  21d
sections.note: The legacy gp2 class uses the in-tree provisioner. Remove its default annotation so only gp3 is default.

sections.title: About this example: snapshot and restore
sections.body: These three manifests use the CSI snapshot feature (the external-snapshotter CRDs and controller must be installed; the EBS CSI add-on can deploy the snapshot controller). The `VolumeSnapshotClass` names the driver, the `VolumeSnapshot` takes a point-in-time copy of `pg-data`, and the last PVC restores it by naming the snapshot in `dataSource`. Look at `READYTOUSE` in the output: do not restore until it is `true`. For consistent database snapshots, quiesce or checkpoint the database first.

sections.code:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-snapclass
driver: ebs.csi.aws.com
deletionPolicy: Retain
---
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: VolumeSnapshot
metadata:
  name: pg-data-20260302
  namespace: orders
spec:
  volumeSnapshotClassName: ebs-snapclass
  source:
    persistentVolumeClaimName: pg-data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pg-data-restored
  namespace: orders
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  storageClassName: gp3
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 50Gi
  dataSource:
    name: pg-data-20260302
    kind: VolumeSnapshot
    apiGroup: snapshot.storage.k8s.io
sections.title: VolumeSnapshotClass, VolumeSnapshot and restore PVC
sections.output:
volumesnapshotclass.snapshot.storage.k8s.io/ebs-snapclass created
volumesnapshot.snapshot.storage.k8s.io/pg-data-20260302 created
persistentvolumeclaim/pg-data-restored created

$ kubectl -n orders get volumesnapshot
NAME               READYTOUSE   SOURCEPVC   SNAPSHOTCLASS   SNAPSHOTCONTENT                                    CREATIONTIME   AGE
pg-data-20260302   true         pg-data     ebs-snapclass   snapcontent-5a3e6f1c-9b2d-4e7a-8c10-2f4d6a8b0c1e   42s            45s
sections.note: The restored volume is created in the zone of the first consuming pod. A snapshot is regional, so it can also seed a volume in another zone.

sections.title: About this example: diagnosing a stuck PVC
sections.body: This is the troubleshooting session for the most common EBS problem, a pod stuck in Pending because its volume lives in a zone with no node capacity. `describe pod` shows the scheduler's message `volume node affinity conflict`, and `get pv` plus the node label reveal the zone mismatch. The fix is capacity in that zone (for Karpenter, allow the zone) or restoring from a snapshot into another zone.

sections.code:
kubectl -n orders describe pod pg-0 | grep -A3 Events
kubectl get pv -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,ZONE:.spec.nodeAffinity.required.nodeSelectorTerms[0].matchExpressions[0].values[0],CLAIM:.spec.claimRef.name
kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone
sections.title: Find the zone conflict
sections.output:
Events:
  Type     Reason            Age   From               Message
  ----     ------            ----  ----               -------
  Warning  FailedScheduling  3m    default-scheduler  0/4 nodes are available: 2 node(s) had volume node affinity conflict, 2 node(s) had untolerated taint {dedicated: gpu}.
NAME                                       ZONE         CLAIM
pvc-6d3f1a2b-7c4e-4d89-b0a1-9e8f7a6b5c4d   us-east-1b   pg-data
NAME                         STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION               ZONE
ip-10-0-14-23.ec2.internal   Ready    <none>   3d    v1.31.2-eks-94953ac   us-east-1a
ip-10-0-35-90.ec2.internal   Ready    <none>   2d    v1.31.2-eks-94953ac   us-east-1c
sections.note: Prevention: run at least one node per zone for every node pool that hosts stateful pods.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** `volumeBindingMode: Immediate` for EBS, which creates volumes in a random zone. **2.** Running a StatefulSet whose nodes exist in only one zone. **3.** Forgetting the IAM role for the CSI driver, so PVCs hang with `AccessDenied` events. **4.** `reclaimPolicy: Delete` on data you cannot lose; use `Retain` and snapshots. **5.** Treating snapshots as the only backup (they live in the same account and region) and not testing a restore. **6.** Using EFS for latency-sensitive databases.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
EBS is fast, zonal, single-writer block storage; EFS is shared, regional file storage. StorageClasses define encryption, IOPS and binding mode, and `WaitForFirstConsumer` keeps volumes next to their pods. CSI snapshots give point-in-time copies you can restore into new PVCs.

Next: seeing what the cluster is doing, with Container Insights, managed Prometheus and Grafana, control plane logs and alarms.

questions.explain: It avoids creating volumes in a zone without usable nodes.

lessons.title: Observability on AWS: logs, metrics and alarms
lessons.summary: Turn on control plane logging, Container Insights and managed Prometheus, and wire alarms that page before users notice.
objectives: Enable and read EKS control plane logs in CloudWatch
Install Container Insights through the CloudWatch Observability add-on
Send Prometheus metrics to Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus and view them in Managed Grafana
Create alarms and Logs Insights queries for the signals that matter

sections.title: Three sources of signals on EKS
sections.body:
You need three kinds of telemetry. **Control plane logs** come from the AWS-managed API server, audit, authenticator, controller manager and scheduler and are shipped to CloudWatch Logs only if you enable them. **Node and pod metrics and logs** come from agents on your nodes: **Container Insights** (the `amazon-cloudwatch-observability` add-on, CloudWatch agent plus Fluent Bit) sends CPU, memory, network and container logs to CloudWatch. **Application and Kubernetes metrics in the Prometheus format** are scraped by Prometheus (or the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry collector) and stored in **Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus** (AMP), then charted in **Amazon Managed Grafana**.

The CloudWatch path is the quickest to enable and integrates with alarms and SNS; the Prometheus path gives PromQL, the Kubernetes community dashboards, and SLO tooling like the one in the Reliability course.

sections.title: Control plane log types
head: Log type
What it contains
Use it for
rows: Who did what (every API request, with user and verb)
Security investigations, who deleted the Deployment
401 or access denied errors, mapping of IAM to Kubernetes users

sections.title: About this example: enable logging and Container Insights
sections.body: These commands turn on the three most useful control plane log types, set a 90-day retention so the log group does not grow forever, and install the CloudWatch Observability add-on with a Pod Identity role. Run them once per cluster (or put the same settings in Terraform with `cluster_enabled_log_types`). In the output look at `status`: `ACTIVE` for the add-on means agents are running on every node, which you confirm with the DaemonSet listing.

sections.code:
aws eks update-cluster-config --name prod-eks \
  --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator"],"enabled":true}]}'
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/eks/prod-eks/cluster --retention-in-days 90
aws eks create-addon --cluster-name prod-eks --addon-name amazon-cloudwatch-observability \
  --pod-identity-associations serviceAccount=cloudwatch-agent,roleArn=arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/CloudWatchAgentRole
kubectl -n amazon-cloudwatch get daemonset
sections.title: Control plane logs, retention and Container Insights
sections.note: Container Insights log ingestion can become your largest CloudWatch cost. Set retention on every log group and filter noisy namespaces.

sections.title: About this example: remote-writing to Managed Prometheus
sections.body: This is a Helm values fragment for the community `prometheus` chart (or `kube-prometheus-stack`) that ships metrics to an AMP workspace. It is a values file, not a Kubernetes manifest, so it is shown as text and used with `helm upgrade --install prometheus prometheus-community/prometheus -n monitoring -f values.yaml`. The ServiceAccount is bound to an IAM role allowed `aps:RemoteWrite`; look at `url`, which must contain your workspace id, and `sigv4`, which signs the request with those AWS credentials. Managed Grafana then uses the AMP workspace as a data source.

sections.code:
serviceAccounts:
  server:
    name: amp-prometheus
    annotations:
      eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/amp-remote-write

server:
  retention: 6h
  remoteWrite:
    - url: https://aps-workspaces.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/workspaces/ws-1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d/api/v1/remote_write
      sigv4:
        region: us-east-1
      queue_config:
        max_samples_per_send: 1000
        max_shards: 200
        capacity: 2500
  persistentVolume:
    enabled: true
    size: 20Gi
sections.title: values.yaml for remote write to AMP
sections.note: Keep local retention short (here 6 hours); AMP stores 150 days by default. The workspace is created with: aws amp create-workspace --alias prod-eks.

sections.title: About this example: an alarm and a Logs Insights query
sections.body: The first command creates a CloudWatch alarm on Container Insights' `node_cpu_utilization`, notifying an SNS topic, and the second runs a **Logs Insights** query on the audit log to find who deleted pods in the last hour. The query output shows the user, verb and object, which is the first thing you need after an unexpected deletion. Check the alarm `StateValue`: `INSUFFICIENT_DATA` right after creation is normal until the first datapoints arrive.

sections.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name prod-eks-node-cpu-high \
  --namespace ContainerInsights --metric-name node_cpu_utilization \
  --dimensions Name=ClusterName,Value=prod-eks --statistic Average --period 300 \
  --evaluation-periods 3 --threshold 85 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:oncall
aws logs start-query --log-group-name /aws/eks/prod-eks/cluster \
  --start-time $(date -d '1 hour ago' +%s) --end-time $(date +%s) \
  --query-string 'fields @timestamp, user.username, verb, objectRef.resource, objectRef.name | filter verb = "delete" and objectRef.resource = "pods" | sort @timestamp desc | limit 5'
aws logs get-query-results --query-id 2b9c7e1a-3d4f-4a5b-8c6d-7e8f9a0b1c2d
sections.title: CloudWatch alarm and audit query
sections.note: Alarm on symptoms (API error rate, pending pods, node NotReady, disk pressure) and send to an SNS topic wired to your pager.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** Enabling every log type with no retention, then being surprised by the CloudWatch bill. **2.** Alerting on CPU only; also alert on `pod_number_of_container_restarts`, pending pods and node NotReady. **3.** Running self-managed Prometheus with a large local volume instead of remote-writing to AMP. **4.** Not enabling the audit log until after an incident. **5.** Giving agents admin IAM instead of `CloudWatchAgentServerPolicy` or `aps:RemoteWrite` only. **6.** Dashboards nobody owns: every alarm needs a runbook link.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Enable control plane logs (api, audit, authenticator) with retention, use the CloudWatch Observability add-on for Container Insights, and remote-write Prometheus metrics to AMP for Managed Grafana. Add alarms with an owner and a runbook, and learn a few Logs Insights queries before you need them.

The final lesson is the operational one: upgrading Kubernetes safely, backing up with Velero, planning disaster recovery, and troubleshooting.

lessons.title: Upgrades, backup, disaster recovery and troubleshooting
lessons.summary: Run a safe EKS version upgrade, back up with Velero, plan for regional failure, and debug the three most common EKS failures.
objectives: Execute the EKS upgrade order: checks, control plane, add-ons, node groups
Find deprecated APIs with pluto or kubent before upgrading
Schedule Velero backups and describe a multi-region recovery strategy
Diagnose nodes that do not join, IP exhaustion and 401 Unauthorized errors

sections.title: Upgrades are routine, so make them boring
sections.body:
EKS supports each Kubernetes minor version for about 14 months in standard support, after which it moves to paid extended support or is force-upgraded. Treat upgrades as a quarterly routine. The rules: you can upgrade the **control plane one minor version at a time**; nodes may lag the control plane by up to three minors (from 1.28 on), but you should upgrade them promptly; and a control plane upgrade **cannot be rolled back**.

The order is always the same: (1) read the release notes and run **deprecated API checks**, (2) test in a non-production cluster, (3) upgrade the control plane, (4) upgrade add-ons (VPC CNI, CoreDNS, kube-proxy, EBS CSI) to versions compatible with the new Kubernetes version, (5) roll the node groups (or let Karpenter replace nodes), (6) verify. The Terraform change is one line: `cluster_version = "1.31"` becomes `"1.32"`.

sections.title: Upgrade runbook at a glance
head: Step
Action
Verify with
rows: Check API deprecations, add-on compatibility, PDBs, free IPs in subnets (5 needed by the control plane)
Terraform apply of the new cluster_version, or aws eks update-cluster-version
Update each add-on to the version compatible with the new minor
Managed node groups: update-nodegroup-version (rolling, respects PDBs). Karpenter: drift replaces nodes after AMI alias update
Workloads healthy, no Pending pods, alerts quiet

sections.title: About this example: preflight checks and the upgrade
sections.body: This session is the real runbook for moving prod-eks from 1.31 to 1.32. `pluto` (Fairwinds) and `kubent` (kube-no-trouble) scan live objects and Helm releases for APIs removed in the target version; `pluto` takes the target version with `--target-versions`. Then the control plane is upgraded and polled until `Successful`, followed by a managed node group rolling update. Read the pluto table first: any row with `REMOVED true` must be fixed before you upgrade, because the object will stop working.

sections.code:
pluto detect-all-in-cluster --target-versions k8s=v1.32.0 -o wide
kubent --target-version 1.32.0
aws eks update-cluster-version --name prod-eks --kubernetes-version 1.32
aws eks describe-update --name prod-eks --update-id 8d4e9a1b-6c2f-4d3e-9a7b-5f1c3e2d4a6b --query update.status
aws eks update-nodegroup-version --cluster-name prod-eks --nodegroup-name system
kubectl get nodes
sections.title: Deprecated API check and upgrade commands
sections.note: The control plane upgrade takes about 10 to 15 minutes; node group rollouts drain one node at a time (maxUnavailable in the update config) and honour PodDisruptionBudgets.

sections.title: About this example: Velero backup schedule
sections.body: **Velero** backs up Kubernetes objects to an S3 bucket and volumes through EBS snapshots (or file-system backup). You install it with Helm using an S3 bucket and a Pod Identity role; this manifest then defines a daily `Schedule` that backs up everything except system namespaces, keeping each backup for 30 days (`ttl`). Apply it with `kubectl apply -f`, then use `velero backup get` to confirm a backup is `Completed`. A backup you have never restored is not a backup, so restore into a scratch cluster at least quarterly with `velero restore create --from-backup`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: daily-prod
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"
  template:
    ttl: 720h0m0s
    includedNamespaces:
      - "*"
    excludedNamespaces:
      - kube-system
      - velero
    snapshotVolumes: true
    storageLocation: default
    volumeSnapshotLocations:
      - default

sections.note: Disaster recovery: the cluster is rebuilt from Terraform, workloads from Git (GitOps) and data from Velero or AWS Backup. For regional failure, copy S3 backups and EBS snapshots to a second region (S3 cross-region replication), keep the Terraform for that region ready, and define RTO/RPO. Active-active needs a global data layer and Route 53 health checks; most teams choose pilot light.

sections.title: About this example: the three classic failures
sections.body: These outputs are what you actually see when something is wrong. **Nodes not joining**: an empty `get nodes` after a node group is `Active`; the cause shown here is a missing access entry or aws-auth role for the node role (`Unauthorized` in kubelet logs). **IP exhaustion**: pods Pending with `failed to assign an IP address to container` because subnets are full. **401 Unauthorized**: `kubectl` fails because your IAM identity has no access entry or the token is for the wrong account. Read the quoted error message in each, it names the fix.

sections.code:
kubectl get nodes
aws eks describe-nodegroup --cluster-name prod-eks --nodegroup-name system --query 'nodegroup.health.issues'
kubectl -n orders describe pod orders-api-7f9c5d8b64-2kq9x | tail -n 4
aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids subnet-0aa1 --query 'Subnets[].AvailableIpAddressCount'
kubectl get pods
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text
aws eks list-access-entries --cluster-name prod-eks
sections.title: Diagnosing join, IP and 401 failures
sections.note: Fixes: join failure - add the node role access entry (type EC2_LINUX) and check security groups and the CNI; IP exhaustion - enable prefix delegation, add secondary CIDR (100.64.0.0/16) with custom networking, or use larger subnets; 401 - create an access entry for your role (Contractor is missing above).

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: **1.** Upgrading add-ons before the control plane, or skipping CoreDNS and kube-proxy. **2.** Skipping the deprecated API scan because the manifests in Git look fine; Helm releases and old live objects matter. **3.** Not checking free IPs: the control plane upgrade needs up to five free IPs in the cluster subnets. **4.** PDBs with `minAvailable` equal to replicas, which blocks node draining forever. **5.** Velero in the same account and region as the only copy. **6.** Debugging 401 by changing RBAC, when the error is authentication (access entry), not authorisation (`403 Forbidden`).

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body:
Upgrade one minor at a time in a fixed order: preflight (`pluto`/`kubent`), control plane, add-ons, nodes, verify. Back up objects and volumes with Velero, test restores, and plan for regional loss with replicated backups plus Terraform and GitOps. When something breaks, read the error: `Unable to join` means access entry or networking, `failed to assign an IP` means subnet space, `Unauthorized` means authentication.

You now have the full production path: identity, Terraform, security, scaling, storage, observability and operations. Continue with the GitOps and Reliability courses to automate delivery and measure service health on top of this foundation.

exercises.title: Scan for deprecated APIs
exercises.prompt: Run pluto against your cluster for the next Kubernetes version.
exercises.expected: A table of deprecated or removed APIs, or none found.
exercises.hint: Fix rows with REMOVED true before upgrading.
exercises.solution: Update manifests/Helm charts to the replacement API, redeploy, then rerun pluto.

exercises.title: Check access entries
exercises.prompt: List who has access to the cluster.
exercises.hint: A 401 from kubectl usually means your role is missing here.
exercises.solution: aws eks create-access-entry --cluster-name prod-eks --principal-arn <role-arn> and associate a policy.

questions.question: How many minor versions can a control plane upgrade jump?
questions.explain: EKS upgrades the control plane one minor version at a time.

questions.question: Which tool scans a cluster for APIs removed in a future version?
questions.explain: pluto and kube-no-trouble detect deprecated and removed APIs.

questions.question: Pods Pending with 'failed to assign an IP address to container' suggests...
questions.explain: The VPC CNI cannot allocate pod IPs because subnets or ENIs are out of addresses.

questions.question: Unauthorized (401) from kubectl means...
options: Authentication failed: no access entry for the identity
questions.explain: 401 is authentication; 403 Forbidden is authorisation.
